# Scenarios

<!-- Generated by TestScenarioDocs in pkg/certtool/scenario_test.go: run go test ./pkg/certtool -run TestScenario -update. -->

`certtool --scenario` writes a commented spec for a common situation to `--output-dir` and generates the certificates in it. The comments in the spec say what every certificate is for and how to install it. To change the certificates, edit the spec and run it with `--spec`.

```bash
certtool --scenario web --organization Acme --organizational-unit Platform --hostnames www.example.com,example.com --output-dir certs
# After editing certs/web.yaml:
certtool --spec certs/web.yaml --output-dir certs
```

- Running the same `--scenario` command again reuses the spec and the certificates. If the spec was edited, it stops and says to use `--spec` instead, so edits are never lost; `--overwrite` replaces the spec and every certificate.
- `--export-spec certs.yaml` only writes the spec, and `--export-spec -` writes it to standard output.
- Separate scenarios with commas, such as `--scenario web,code-sign`. Each adds its own top-level entries, and every file name starts with the scenario name, so they can share an output directory. The `kubernetes` scenario is the exception: it uses kubeadm's file names.
- The subject flags (`--organization`, `--country`, and so on), `--key-type`, and `--validity` set the leaf certificates. CAs keep their own key types and validities. A flag that none of the chosen scenarios uses is an error.
- With `--yubikey`, the root CA is left out because it is on the YubiKey: the CAs below it become top-level entries, which the YubiKey signs.
- Each scenario is a template in [pkg/certtool/scenario](../pkg/certtool/scenario), whose data is the flags above.
- Every `.pfx` reads its password from the `CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD` environment variable when the spec is generated. The spec never holds a password.
- Running the spec again reuses the certificates already in the output directory, so you can add entries later. See [Running a spec again](spec.md#running-a-spec-again).

| Scenario | Makes |
| -------- | ----- |
| [`web`](#web) | A root CA and an issuing CA, name constrained to the hostnames, and a server certificate for websites and APIs. |
| [`local-dev`](#local-dev) | A self-signed certificate for localhost and development hostnames. |
| [`mtls`](#mtls) | A root CA and an issuing CA that sign a server certificate and client certificates for mutual TLS, such as gRPC. |
| [`microservices`](#microservices) | A root CA and an issuing CA that sign one certificate per service, used both to serve and to call the other services. |
| [`database`](#database) | A CA that signs a server certificate per database host and client certificates for database users (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB). |
| [`active-directory`](#active-directory) | An enterprise root CA and issuing CA that sign LDAPS certificates for Active Directory domain controllers, with .pfx files to import. |
| [`kubernetes`](#kubernetes) | The certificates kubeadm puts in /etc/kubernetes/pki: the cluster, front proxy, and etcd CAs and the certificates they sign. |
| [`vpn`](#vpn) | A CA that signs a VPN gateway certificate and client certificates, for OpenVPN and IKEv2/IPsec (strongSwan, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android). |
| [`eap-tls`](#eap-tls) | A CA that signs a RADIUS server certificate and client certificates for 802.1X EAP-TLS on Wi-Fi and wired networks. |
| [`iot`](#iot) | A root CA and a device CA that sign an MQTT broker certificate and long-lived device certificates. |
| [`kafka`](#kafka) | A CA that signs a certificate per Kafka broker, with PKCS#12 keystores, and client certificates. |
| [`docker`](#docker) | A CA that signs a Docker daemon certificate and client certificates, to protect the Docker API on port 2376. |
| [`git`](#git) | Certificates for a Git server over HTTPS, and identities that sign commits with S/MIME or SSH and log in with a certificate or an SSH key. |
| [`ssh`](#ssh) | SSH keys for SSH, SFTP, SCP, and rsync: host keys that clients pin in known_hosts, and user keys for authorized_keys. |
| [`ftps`](#ftps) | A CA that signs an FTPS (FTP over TLS) server certificate and optional client certificates, for vsftpd, ProFTPD, and FileZilla Server. |
| [`ios`](#ios) | A development CA for iPhone and iPad apps, a backend certificate that meets Apple's TLS rules, and client identities. |
| [`android`](#android) | A development CA that Android apps trust through a network security config, a backend certificate, and client certificates. |
| [`android-signing`](#android-signing) | An Android app signing (upload) key in a PKCS#12 keystore, valid for 25 years. |
| [`code-sign`](#code-sign) | A code signing certificate for Windows (signtool) or Linux (osslsigncode). |
| [`proxy`](#proxy) | A CA for a TLS-inspecting proxy (Squid, mitmproxy), which signs a certificate for each site on the fly. |

Other systems fit one of these: `web` for OpenLDAP, mail servers, and Elasticsearch over HTTPS; `git` for Subversion and Mercurial over HTTPS; `ssh` for SFTP-only accounts and rsync backups; `mtls` for gRPC; `microservices` for a service mesh without its own CA.

## web

A root CA and an issuing CA, name constrained to the hostnames, and a server certificate for websites and APIs.

- `--hostnames`: the names of the server certificate, which also become the CA's name constraints.

```bash
certtool --scenario web --organization Acme --hostnames www.example.com,example.com --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/web.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario web, written by:
#   certtool --scenario web --organization Acme --hostnames www.example.com,example.com --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/web.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario web: A root CA and an issuing CA, name constrained to the hostnames, and a server certificate for websites and APIs.

# Root CA. Install web-root-ca.crt in the trust store of every client: the operating system, the browser, or the HTTP client's CA bundle.
# Its key can sign anything below it, so move web-root-ca.key offline once the issuing CA exists,
# or keep the root on a YubiKey: certtool --scenario web --yubikey.
- commonName: Acme Web Root CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: web-root-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - www.example.com
    - example.com
  children:
    # Issuing CA: signs the day-to-day certificates. Renew it well before it expires, because a certificate is only valid
    # while its issuers are.
    - commonName: Acme Web Issuing CA
      certificateAuthority: true
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # 3 years.
      validity: 26280h
      organization: Acme
      filename: web-issuing-ca
      children:
        # Server certificate for the hostnames, valid for 90 days. nginx: ssl_certificate takes web-server.crt followed by
        # web-issuing-ca.crt in one file, and ssl_certificate_key takes web-server.key.
        # To add a server, copy this entry with a new commonName, hostnames, and filename.
        - commonName: www.example.com
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          # To renew, delete web-server.crt and web-server.key, then run the spec again.
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          hostnames:
            - www.example.com
            - example.com
          filename: web-server
```

## local-dev

A self-signed certificate for localhost and development hostnames.

- `--hostnames`: optional, development names to add to localhost, such as myapp.localhost.

```bash
certtool --scenario local-dev --organization Acme --hostnames myapp.localhost --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/local-dev.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario local-dev, written by:
#   certtool --scenario local-dev --organization Acme --hostnames myapp.localhost --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/local-dev.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario local-dev: A self-signed certificate for localhost and development hostnames.

# Self-signed certificate for this machine. certtool adds localhost and 127.0.0.1 itself.
# Trust local-dev.crt only on the machine that holds local-dev.key; see docs/use-cases/local-development.md.
- commonName: myapp.localhost
  keyType: ECDSA-256
  validity: 8760h
  organization: Acme
  # Add the names you browse to, such as myapp.localhost.
  hostnames:
    - myapp.localhost
    - ::1
  filename: local-dev
```

## mtls

A root CA and an issuing CA that sign a server certificate and client certificates for mutual TLS, such as gRPC.

- `--hostnames`: the names of the server certificate.
- `--clients`: the names of the client certificates, such as billing,orders.

```bash
certtool --scenario mtls --organization Acme --hostnames api.internal.example.com --clients billing,orders --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/mtls.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario mtls, written by:
#   certtool --scenario mtls --organization Acme --hostnames api.internal.example.com --clients billing,orders --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/mtls.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario mtls: A root CA and an issuing CA that sign a server certificate and client certificates for mutual TLS, such as gRPC.

# Root CA. Both sides trust mtls-root-ca.crt: the server to verify clients, and the clients to verify the server.
# Its key can sign anything below it, so move mtls-root-ca.key offline once the issuing CA exists,
# or keep the root on a YubiKey: certtool --scenario mtls --yubikey.
- commonName: Acme mTLS Root CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: mtls-root-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - api.internal.example.com
  children:
    # Issuing CA: signs the day-to-day certificates. Renew it well before it expires, because a certificate is only valid
    # while its issuers are.
    - commonName: Acme mTLS Issuing CA
      certificateAuthority: true
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # 3 years.
      validity: 26280h
      organization: Acme
      filename: mtls-issuing-ca
      children:
        # Server certificate. Require a client certificate that chains to the root: nginx ssl_verify_client on with
        # ssl_client_certificate mtls-root-ca.crt, or in Go tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert with the root in ClientCAs.
        # Present mtls-server.crt followed by mtls-issuing-ca.crt, so the other side only needs to trust the root.
        - commonName: api.internal.example.com
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          # To renew, delete mtls-server.crt and mtls-server.key, then run the spec again.
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          hostnames:
            - api.internal.example.com
          filename: mtls-server
        # Client certificate for billing, valid for 90 days. The server sees billing as the subject common name:
        # authorize on it, not just on the CA. To use it from a browser, add pfx: modern.
        # Present mtls-client-billing.crt followed by mtls-issuing-ca.crt, so the other side only needs to trust the root.
        - commonName: billing
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          filename: mtls-client-billing
        # Client certificate for orders, valid for 90 days. The server sees orders as the subject common name:
        # authorize on it, not just on the CA. To use it from a browser, add pfx: modern.
        # Present mtls-client-orders.crt followed by mtls-issuing-ca.crt, so the other side only needs to trust the root.
        - commonName: orders
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          filename: mtls-client-orders
```

## microservices

A root CA and an issuing CA that sign one certificate per service, used both to serve and to call the other services.

- `--hostnames`: the DNS name of each service, one certificate each, such as api.platform.svc.cluster.local.

```bash
certtool --scenario microservices --organization Acme --hostnames api.platform.svc.cluster.local,orders.platform.svc.cluster.local,payments.platform.svc.cluster.local --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/microservices.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario microservices, written by:
#   certtool --scenario microservices --organization Acme --hostnames api.platform.svc.cluster.local,orders.platform.svc.cluster.local,payments.platform.svc.cluster.local --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/microservices.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario microservices: A root CA and an issuing CA that sign one certificate per service, used both to serve and to call the other services.

# Root CA. Every service trusts microservices-root-ca.crt to verify its peers, and requires a client certificate from them.
# Its key can sign anything below it, so move microservices-root-ca.key offline once the issuing CA exists,
# or keep the root on a YubiKey: certtool --scenario microservices --yubikey.
- commonName: Acme Services Root CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: microservices-root-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - api.platform.svc.cluster.local
    - orders.platform.svc.cluster.local
    - payments.platform.svc.cluster.local
  children:
    # Issuing CA: signs the day-to-day certificates. Renew it well before it expires, because a certificate is only valid
    # while its issuers are.
    - commonName: Acme Services Issuing CA
      certificateAuthority: true
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # 3 years.
      validity: 26280h
      organization: Acme
      filename: microservices-issuing-ca
      children:
        # Certificate for the service api.platform.svc.cluster.local. The service serves with it and presents it when it calls other services,
        # because certtool's TLS certificates are valid for both. Authorize callers by name, not just by the CA.
        # Present microservices-api-platform-svc-cluster-local.crt followed by microservices-issuing-ca.crt, so the other side only needs to trust the root.
        - commonName: api.platform.svc.cluster.local
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          # To renew, delete microservices-api-platform-svc-cluster-local.crt and microservices-api-platform-svc-cluster-local.key, then run the spec again.
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          hostnames:
            - api.platform.svc.cluster.local
          filename: microservices-api-platform-svc-cluster-local
        # Certificate for the service orders.platform.svc.cluster.local. The service serves with it and presents it when it calls other services,
        # because certtool's TLS certificates are valid for both. Authorize callers by name, not just by the CA.
        # Present microservices-orders-platform-svc-cluster-local.crt followed by microservices-issuing-ca.crt, so the other side only needs to trust the root.
        - commonName: orders.platform.svc.cluster.local
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          # To renew, delete microservices-orders-platform-svc-cluster-local.crt and microservices-orders-platform-svc-cluster-local.key, then run the spec again.
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          hostnames:
            - orders.platform.svc.cluster.local
          filename: microservices-orders-platform-svc-cluster-local
        # Certificate for the service payments.platform.svc.cluster.local. The service serves with it and presents it when it calls other services,
        # because certtool's TLS certificates are valid for both. Authorize callers by name, not just by the CA.
        # Present microservices-payments-platform-svc-cluster-local.crt followed by microservices-issuing-ca.crt, so the other side only needs to trust the root.
        - commonName: payments.platform.svc.cluster.local
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          # To renew, delete microservices-payments-platform-svc-cluster-local.crt and microservices-payments-platform-svc-cluster-local.key, then run the spec again.
          validity: 2160h
          organization: Acme
          hostnames:
            - payments.platform.svc.cluster.local
          filename: microservices-payments-platform-svc-cluster-local
```

## database

A CA that signs a server certificate per database host and client certificates for database users (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB).

- `--hostnames`: the name of each database server, one certificate each.
- `--clients`: optional, database users that log in with a certificate.

```bash
certtool --scenario database --organization Acme --hostnames postgres.internal.example.com,redis.internal.example.com --clients app --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/database.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario database, written by:
#   certtool --scenario database --organization Acme --hostnames postgres.internal.example.com,redis.internal.example.com --clients app --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/database.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario database: A CA that signs a server certificate per database host and client certificates for database users (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB).

# CA. Clients verify the servers with database-ca.crt: PostgreSQL sslrootcert with sslmode=verify-full, MySQL ssl-ca
# with ssl-mode=VERIFY_IDENTITY, Redis tls-ca-cert-file, MongoDB tlsCAFile.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep database-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Database CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: database-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - postgres.internal.example.com
    - redis.internal.example.com
  children:
    # Server certificate for postgres.internal.example.com. PostgreSQL: ssl_cert_file and ssl_key_file (the key must belong to the postgres user).
    # MySQL: ssl_cert and ssl_key. Redis: tls-cert-file and tls-key-file. MongoDB: tlsCertificateKeyFile takes the
    # certificate and key in one file: cat database-postgres-internal-example-com.crt database-postgres-internal-example-com.key > database-postgres-internal-example-com.pem.
    - commonName: postgres.internal.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete database-postgres-internal-example-com.crt and database-postgres-internal-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - postgres.internal.example.com
      filename: database-postgres-internal-example-com
    # Server certificate for redis.internal.example.com. PostgreSQL: ssl_cert_file and ssl_key_file (the key must belong to the postgres user).
    # MySQL: ssl_cert and ssl_key. Redis: tls-cert-file and tls-key-file. MongoDB: tlsCertificateKeyFile takes the
    # certificate and key in one file: cat database-redis-internal-example-com.crt database-redis-internal-example-com.key > database-redis-internal-example-com.pem.
    - commonName: redis.internal.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete database-redis-internal-example-com.crt and database-redis-internal-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - redis.internal.example.com
      filename: database-redis-internal-example-com
    # Client certificate for the database user app, whose user name is the common name. PostgreSQL logs it in with
    # the cert method in pg_hba.conf (hostssl all app all cert); MySQL with CREATE USER ... REQUIRE SUBJECT.
    - commonName: app
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: database-user-app
```

## active-directory

An enterprise root CA and issuing CA that sign LDAPS certificates for Active Directory domain controllers, with .pfx files to import.

- `--hostnames`: the FQDN of each domain controller, such as dc01.corp.example.com.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario active-directory --organization Acme --hostnames dc01.corp.example.com,dc02.corp.example.com --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/active-directory.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario active-directory, written by:
#   certtool --scenario active-directory --organization Acme --hostnames dc01.corp.example.com,dc02.corp.example.com --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/active-directory.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario active-directory: An enterprise root CA and issuing CA that sign LDAPS certificates for Active Directory domain controllers, with .pfx files to import.

# Root CA. Publish active-directory-root-ca.crt to every domain member with Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Policies >
# Windows Settings > Security Settings > Public Key Policies > Trusted Root Certification Authorities), or with
# certutil -dspublish -f active-directory-root-ca.crt RootCA, and the issuing CA with
# certutil -dspublish -f active-directory-issuing-ca.crt SubCA. RSA keys, because some LDAP clients do not accept ECDSA.
# Its key can sign anything below it, so move active-directory-root-ca.key offline once the issuing CA exists,
# or keep the root on a YubiKey: certtool --scenario active-directory --yubikey.
- commonName: Acme Enterprise Root CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: RSA-4096
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: active-directory-root-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - corp.example.com
  children:
    # Issuing CA: signs the day-to-day certificates. Renew it well before it expires, because a certificate is only valid
    # while its issuers are.
    - commonName: Acme Enterprise Issuing CA
      certificateAuthority: true
      keyType: RSA-4096
      # 3 years.
      validity: 26280h
      organization: Acme
      filename: active-directory-issuing-ca
      children:
        # LDAPS certificate for the domain controller dc01.corp.example.com. On it, in an administrator PowerShell:
        #   Import-PfxCertificate -FilePath active-directory-dc01-corp-example-com.pfx -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\My `
        #     -Password (ConvertTo-SecureString $env:CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD -AsPlainText -Force)
        # The DC uses it for LDAPS on port 636, and 3269 for the global catalog, within minutes or after a restart.
        # Check with: openssl s_client -connect dc01.corp.example.com:636 -CAfile active-directory-root-ca.crt
        - commonName: dc01.corp.example.com
          pfx: modern
          pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
          keyType: RSA-2048
          # To renew, delete active-directory-dc01-corp-example-com.crt and active-directory-dc01-corp-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
          # Then import the new .pfx and delete the old certificate from the store.
          validity: 8760h
          organization: Acme
          # The DC's name, and the domain name, so clients that connect to corp.example.com reach any DC.
          hostnames:
            - dc01.corp.example.com
            - corp.example.com
          filename: active-directory-dc01-corp-example-com
        # LDAPS certificate for the domain controller dc02.corp.example.com. On it, in an administrator PowerShell:
        #   Import-PfxCertificate -FilePath active-directory-dc02-corp-example-com.pfx -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\My `
        #     -Password (ConvertTo-SecureString $env:CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD -AsPlainText -Force)
        # The DC uses it for LDAPS on port 636, and 3269 for the global catalog, within minutes or after a restart.
        # Check with: openssl s_client -connect dc02.corp.example.com:636 -CAfile active-directory-root-ca.crt
        - commonName: dc02.corp.example.com
          pfx: modern
          pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
          keyType: RSA-2048
          # To renew, delete active-directory-dc02-corp-example-com.crt and active-directory-dc02-corp-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
          # Then import the new .pfx and delete the old certificate from the store.
          validity: 8760h
          organization: Acme
          # The DC's name, and the domain name, so clients that connect to corp.example.com reach any DC.
          hostnames:
            - dc02.corp.example.com
            - corp.example.com
          filename: active-directory-dc02-corp-example-com
```

## kubernetes

The certificates kubeadm puts in /etc/kubernetes/pki: the cluster, front proxy, and etcd CAs and the certificates they sign.

- `--hostnames`: the control-plane node name first, then its IP addresses and any load balancer name.

```bash
certtool --scenario kubernetes --organization Acme --hostnames cp1,192.168.1.100,k8s-api.example.com --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/kubernetes.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario kubernetes, written by:
#   certtool --scenario kubernetes --organization Acme --hostnames cp1,192.168.1.100,k8s-api.example.com --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/kubernetes.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario kubernetes: The certificates kubeadm puts in /etc/kubernetes/pki: the cluster, front proxy, and etcd CAs and the certificates they sign.

# Cluster CA. The file names are kubeadm's: generate with --output-dir /etc/kubernetes/pki on the first control-plane
# node, move the etcd files as the etcd CA says, then run kubeadm init. kubeadm uses these certificates and makes
# the kubeconfig files, the service account key pair (sa.key, sa.pub), and anything else that is missing.
# Kubernetes reads a client certificate's organization as a group, so do not bind RBAC roles to Acme.
- commonName: kubernetes
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: RSA-2048
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: ca
  children:
    # API server certificate.
    - commonName: kube-apiserver
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      # Every name and address clients use for the API server: the node, a load balancer, and the first address of
      # the service CIDR (10.96.0.1 for kubeadm's default 10.96.0.0/12). Change cluster.local if the cluster domain differs.
      hostnames:
        - cp1
        - 192.168.1.100
        - k8s-api.example.com
        - kubernetes
        - kubernetes.default
        - kubernetes.default.svc
        - kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
        - 10.96.0.1
      filename: apiserver
    # The client certificate the API server presents to kubelets.
    - commonName: kube-apiserver-kubelet-client
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      # A Kubernetes group: system:masters may always use the kubelet API.
      organization: system:masters
      filename: apiserver-kubelet-client
# Front proxy CA for the aggregation layer (--requestheader-client-ca-file). kubeadm keeps it separate from the
# cluster CA, so a front proxy certificate cannot be used as a user's client certificate.
- commonName: front-proxy-ca
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: RSA-2048
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: front-proxy-ca
  children:
    # The client certificate the API server presents to extension API servers.
    - commonName: front-proxy-client
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: front-proxy-client
# etcd CA. kubeadm reads the etcd certificates from /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/: move etcd-ca, etcd-server, etcd-peer,
# and etcd-healthcheck-client (.crt and .key) there as ca, server, peer, and healthcheck-client.
- commonName: etcd-ca
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: RSA-2048
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: etcd-ca
  children:
    # etcd server certificate, named after the node.
    - commonName: cp1
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - cp1
        - 192.168.1.100
        - k8s-api.example.com
        - ::1
      filename: etcd-server
    # etcd peer certificate, for the other members of the etcd cluster. Its hostnames are the node's addresses.
    - commonName: cp1
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - cp1
        - 192.168.1.100
        - k8s-api.example.com
      filename: etcd-peer
    # Client certificate for the etcd liveness probe.
    - commonName: kube-etcd-healthcheck-client
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: etcd-healthcheck-client
    # The client certificate the API server presents to etcd. It stays in /etc/kubernetes/pki.
    - commonName: kube-apiserver-etcd-client
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: apiserver-etcd-client
```

## vpn

A CA that signs a VPN gateway certificate and client certificates, for OpenVPN and IKEv2/IPsec (strongSwan, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android).

- `--hostnames`: the names and addresses clients connect to the gateway by.
- `--clients`: the users or devices that connect, one certificate each.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario vpn --organization Acme --hostnames vpn.example.com,203.0.113.10 --clients alice,bob --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/vpn.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario vpn, written by:
#   certtool --scenario vpn --organization Acme --hostnames vpn.example.com,203.0.113.10 --clients alice,bob --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/vpn.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario vpn: A CA that signs a VPN gateway certificate and client certificates, for OpenVPN and IKEv2/IPsec (strongSwan, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android).

# CA. Gateways and clients trust vpn-ca.crt (OpenVPN: ca; strongSwan: /etc/swanctl/x509ca).
# certtool does not make CRLs, so keep client certificates short-lived; OpenVPN needs a CRL to revoke one early.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep vpn-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme VPN CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: vpn-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - vpn.example.com
  # The IP addresses certificates below this CA may use.
  permittedIPRanges:
    - 203.0.113.10/32
  children:
    # Gateway certificate. OpenVPN: cert vpn-gateway.crt and key vpn-gateway.key. strongSwan: /etc/swanctl/x509 and private.
    # IKEv2 clients on Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android check that the name they connect to is in hostnames.
    # To add a gateway, copy this entry with a new commonName, hostnames, and filename.
    - commonName: vpn.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete vpn-gateway.crt and vpn-gateway.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - vpn.example.com
        - 203.0.113.10
      filename: vpn-gateway
    # Client certificate for alice, valid for 180 days. OpenVPN clients use the .crt and .key; Windows, macOS, iOS, and
    # Android import vpn-client-alice.pfx. Every certtool TLS certificate is also valid for server authentication, so make
    # OpenVPN clients check the gateway's name with verify-x509-name vpn.example.com name, not only remote-cert-tls server.
    - commonName: alice
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 4380h
      organization: Acme
      filename: vpn-client-alice
    # Client certificate for bob, valid for 180 days. OpenVPN clients use the .crt and .key; Windows, macOS, iOS, and
    # Android import vpn-client-bob.pfx. Every certtool TLS certificate is also valid for server authentication, so make
    # OpenVPN clients check the gateway's name with verify-x509-name vpn.example.com name, not only remote-cert-tls server.
    - commonName: bob
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 4380h
      organization: Acme
      filename: vpn-client-bob
```

## eap-tls

A CA that signs a RADIUS server certificate and client certificates for 802.1X EAP-TLS on Wi-Fi and wired networks.

- `--hostnames`: the name of the RADIUS server, which supplicants check.
- `--clients`: the users or devices that join the network, one certificate each.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario eap-tls --organization Acme --hostnames radius.corp.example.com --clients alice-laptop,bob-phone --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/eap-tls.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario eap-tls, written by:
#   certtool --scenario eap-tls --organization Acme --hostnames radius.corp.example.com --clients alice-laptop,bob-phone --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/eap-tls.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario eap-tls: A CA that signs a RADIUS server certificate and client certificates for 802.1X EAP-TLS on Wi-Fi and wired networks.

# CA. Configure every supplicant to trust only eap-tls-ca.crt for this network and to check the RADIUS server's name;
# otherwise anyone with a certificate from another CA the device trusts could pose as the network.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep eap-tls-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Network Access CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: eap-tls-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - radius.corp.example.com
  children:
    # RADIUS server certificate. FreeRADIUS: certificate_file, private_key_file, and ca_file in mods-available/eap.
    # Windows NPS: import eap-tls-radius.pfx into the computer's Personal store and choose it in the network policy.
    - commonName: radius.corp.example.com
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete eap-tls-radius.crt and eap-tls-radius.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - radius.corp.example.com
      filename: eap-tls-radius
    # Client certificate for alice-laptop. Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android import eap-tls-client-alice-laptop.pfx, or an MDM pushes it
    # with the Wi-Fi profile. Linux wpa_supplicant uses client_cert and private_key. RADIUS can authorize on the common name.
    - commonName: alice-laptop
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: eap-tls-client-alice-laptop
    # Client certificate for bob-phone. Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android import eap-tls-client-bob-phone.pfx, or an MDM pushes it
    # with the Wi-Fi profile. Linux wpa_supplicant uses client_cert and private_key. RADIUS can authorize on the common name.
    - commonName: bob-phone
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: eap-tls-client-bob-phone
```

## iot

A root CA and a device CA that sign an MQTT broker certificate and long-lived device certificates.

- `--hostnames`: the names of the MQTT broker.
- `--clients`: the device IDs, one certificate each.

```bash
certtool --scenario iot --organization Acme --hostnames mqtt.example.com --clients sensor-0001,sensor-0002 --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/iot.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario iot, written by:
#   certtool --scenario iot --organization Acme --hostnames mqtt.example.com --clients sensor-0001,sensor-0002 --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/iot.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario iot: A root CA and a device CA that sign an MQTT broker certificate and long-lived device certificates.

# Root CA. The broker trusts iot-root-ca.crt to verify devices, and every device carries it to verify the broker.
# Its key can sign anything below it, so move iot-root-ca.key offline once the issuing CA exists,
# or keep the root on a YubiKey: certtool --scenario iot --yubikey.
- commonName: Acme Device Root CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: iot-root-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - mqtt.example.com
  children:
    # Issuing CA: signs the day-to-day certificates. Renew it well before it expires, because a certificate is only valid
    # while its issuers are.
    - commonName: Acme Device Issuing CA
      certificateAuthority: true
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # 3 years.
      validity: 26280h
      organization: Acme
      filename: iot-issuing-ca
      children:
        # MQTT broker certificate. In the broker's configuration: cafile iot-root-ca.crt, certfile (this certificate followed by iot-issuing-ca.crt),
        # keyfile, require_certificate true, and use_identity_as_username true, which makes each device's common name its user.
        - commonName: mqtt.example.com
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          # To renew, delete iot-broker.crt and iot-broker.key, then run the spec again.
          validity: 8760h
          organization: Acme
          hostnames:
            - mqtt.example.com
          filename: iot-broker
        # Device certificate for sensor-0001. Provision the device with iot-device-sensor-0001.crt, iot-device-sensor-0001.key, iot-issuing-ca.crt,
        # and iot-root-ca.crt. Valid for 5 years, because devices are hard to reach; plan how to replace it before then.
        - commonName: sensor-0001
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          validity: 43800h
          organization: Acme
          filename: iot-device-sensor-0001
        # Device certificate for sensor-0002. Provision the device with iot-device-sensor-0002.crt, iot-device-sensor-0002.key, iot-issuing-ca.crt,
        # and iot-root-ca.crt. Valid for 5 years, because devices are hard to reach; plan how to replace it before then.
        - commonName: sensor-0002
          keyType: ECDSA-256
          validity: 43800h
          organization: Acme
          filename: iot-device-sensor-0002
```

## kafka

A CA that signs a certificate per Kafka broker, with PKCS#12 keystores, and client certificates.

- `--hostnames`: the name of each broker, one certificate each.
- `--clients`: optional, the Kafka clients that authenticate with a certificate.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario kafka --organization Acme --hostnames kafka-1.example.com,kafka-2.example.com,kafka-3.example.com --clients orders-service --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/kafka.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario kafka, written by:
#   certtool --scenario kafka --organization Acme --hostnames kafka-1.example.com,kafka-2.example.com,kafka-3.example.com --clients orders-service --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/kafka.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario kafka: A CA that signs a certificate per Kafka broker, with PKCS#12 keystores, and client certificates.

# CA. Brokers and clients trust kafka-ca.crt: ssl.truststore.type=PEM and ssl.truststore.location=kafka-ca.crt.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep kafka-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Kafka CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: kafka-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - kafka-1.example.com
    - kafka-2.example.com
    - kafka-3.example.com
  children:
    # Broker certificate for kafka-1.example.com. In server.properties: ssl.keystore.type=PKCS12, ssl.keystore.location=kafka-kafka-1-example-com.pfx,
    # ssl.keystore.password and ssl.key.password set to the .pfx password, and ssl.client.auth=required for mutual TLS.
    - commonName: kafka-1.example.com
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete kafka-kafka-1-example-com.crt and kafka-kafka-1-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - kafka-1.example.com
      filename: kafka-kafka-1-example-com
    # Broker certificate for kafka-2.example.com. In server.properties: ssl.keystore.type=PKCS12, ssl.keystore.location=kafka-kafka-2-example-com.pfx,
    # ssl.keystore.password and ssl.key.password set to the .pfx password, and ssl.client.auth=required for mutual TLS.
    - commonName: kafka-2.example.com
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete kafka-kafka-2-example-com.crt and kafka-kafka-2-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - kafka-2.example.com
      filename: kafka-kafka-2-example-com
    # Broker certificate for kafka-3.example.com. In server.properties: ssl.keystore.type=PKCS12, ssl.keystore.location=kafka-kafka-3-example-com.pfx,
    # ssl.keystore.password and ssl.key.password set to the .pfx password, and ssl.client.auth=required for mutual TLS.
    - commonName: kafka-3.example.com
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete kafka-kafka-3-example-com.crt and kafka-kafka-3-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - kafka-3.example.com
      filename: kafka-kafka-3-example-com
    # Client certificate for orders-service, in kafka-client-orders-service.pfx for the client's ssl.keystore.location. Kafka's principal is the
    # whole subject (User:CN=orders-service,O=...); to use the common name in ACLs, set
    # ssl.principal.mapping.rules=RULE:^CN=([^,]+).*$/$1/,DEFAULT on the brokers.
    - commonName: orders-service
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: kafka-client-orders-service
```

## docker

A CA that signs a Docker daemon certificate and client certificates, to protect the Docker API on port 2376.

- `--hostnames`: the names and addresses of the Docker host.
- `--clients`: optional, the clients that may use the Docker API; one named docker-client when not given.

```bash
certtool --scenario docker --organization Acme --hostnames docker-host.example.com,192.168.1.50 --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/docker.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario docker, written by:
#   certtool --scenario docker --organization Acme --hostnames docker-host.example.com,192.168.1.50 --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/docker.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario docker: A CA that signs a Docker daemon certificate and client certificates, to protect the Docker API on port 2376.

# CA. The daemon trusts docker-ca.crt to verify clients, and clients trust it to verify the daemon.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep docker-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Docker CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: docker-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - docker-host.example.com
  # The IP addresses certificates below this CA may use.
  permittedIPRanges:
    - 192.168.1.50/32
  children:
    # Docker daemon certificate. dockerd --tlsverify --tlscacert=docker-ca.crt --tlscert=docker-daemon.crt
    # --tlskey=docker-daemon.key -H=0.0.0.0:2376, or the same settings in /etc/docker/daemon.json.
    - commonName: docker-host.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete docker-daemon.crt and docker-daemon.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - docker-host.example.com
        - 192.168.1.50
      filename: docker-daemon
    # Client certificate for docker-client. Anyone who has it controls the Docker host. Copy docker-ca.crt, docker-client-docker-client.crt,
    # and docker-client-docker-client.key to ~/.docker as ca.pem, cert.pem, and key.pem, then run: docker --tlsverify -H=docker-host.example.com:2376 version
    - commonName: docker-client
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: docker-client-docker-client
```

## git

Certificates for a Git server over HTTPS, and identities that sign commits with S/MIME or SSH and log in with a certificate or an SSH key.

- `--hostnames`: the names of the Git server (Gitea, GitLab, Bitbucket, or nginx in front of git http-backend).
- `--clients`: optional, people, by email address such as `alice@example.com`, who sign commits; and machines, such as ci, that only log in.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario git --organization Acme --hostnames git.example.com --clients alice@example.com,bob@example.com,ci --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/git.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario git, written by:
#   certtool --scenario git --organization Acme --hostnames git.example.com --clients alice@example.com,bob@example.com,ci --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/git.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario git: Certificates for a Git server over HTTPS, and identities that sign commits with S/MIME or SSH and log in with a certificate or an SSH key.

# CA. Clients trust git-ca.crt for the server: git config --global http.https://git.example.com/.sslCAInfo git-ca.crt.
# Subversion: ssl-authority-files in ~/.subversion/servers. Mercurial: git.example.com:verifycertsfile under [hostsecurity].
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep git-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Git CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: git-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - git.example.com
  children:
    # Server certificate for git.example.com. Gitea: CERT_FILE git-server-git-example-com.crt and KEY_FILE git-server-git-example-com.key
    # under [server] with PROTOCOL = https. GitLab: nginx['ssl_certificate'] and nginx['ssl_certificate_key'] in gitlab.rb.
    # Bitbucket, or nginx in front of git http-backend: ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key.
    - commonName: git.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete git-server-git-example-com.crt and git-server-git-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - git.example.com
      filename: git-server-git-example-com
# CA. Signs the people and machines below, and has no name constraints because gpgsm refuses chains that have them.
# S/MIME signing with gpgsm: gpgsm --import git-identity-ca.crt, add its fingerprint followed by "S relax" to
# ~/.gnupg/trustlist.txt, and add disable-crl-checks to ~/.gnupg/gpgsm.conf, because certtool makes no CRLs. Then for each
# person: gpgsm --import their .pfx, and git config gpg.format x509, gpg.x509.program gpgsm, and user.signingkey <their email>.
# On Windows and macOS, import the .pfx into the certificate store or Keychain and use gpg.x509.program smimesign instead.
# SSH signing: git config gpg.format ssh and user.signingkey <their .key>; verifiers list each person in
# gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile as <email> followed by the type and data in their .key.pub. GitHub marks S/MIME commits verified
# only when a public CA issued the certificate, so use SSH signing there.
# HTTPS logins with a certificate: git config http.sslCert <.crt> and http.sslKey <.key>, and on nginx ssl_verify_client on
# with ssl_client_certificate git-identity-ca.crt.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep git-identity-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Git Identity CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: git-identity-ca
  children:
    # alice@example.com, who signs commits as git config user.email alice@example.com. gpgsm imports git-person-alice-example-com.pfx;
    # for SSH, add git-person-alice-example-com.key.pub to the Git server as both an authentication and a signing key.
    - commonName: alice@example.com
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete git-person-alice-example-com.crt and git-person-alice-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      emailAddresses:
        - alice@example.com
      sshPublicKey: true
      filename: git-person-alice-example-com
    # bob@example.com, who signs commits as git config user.email bob@example.com. gpgsm imports git-person-bob-example-com.pfx;
    # for SSH, add git-person-bob-example-com.key.pub to the Git server as both an authentication and a signing key.
    - commonName: bob@example.com
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete git-person-bob-example-com.crt and git-person-bob-example-com.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      emailAddresses:
        - bob@example.com
      sshPublicKey: true
      filename: git-person-bob-example-com
    # The machine ci, such as a CI runner, valid for 90 days. Add git-machine-ci.key.pub to the repository as a
    # deploy key and clone with GIT_SSH_COMMAND="ssh -i git-machine-ci.key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes", or log in over HTTPS with the certificate.
    - commonName: ci
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete git-machine-ci.crt and git-machine-ci.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 2160h
      organization: Acme
      sshPublicKey: true
      filename: git-machine-ci
```

## ssh

SSH keys for SSH, SFTP, SCP, and rsync: host keys that clients pin in known_hosts, and user keys for authorized_keys.

- `--hostnames`: optional, the SSH or SFTP servers, one host key each.
- `--clients`: the users or automation accounts that log in, one key each.

```bash
certtool --scenario ssh --organization Acme --hostnames sftp.example.com,bastion.example.com --clients alice,backup --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/ssh.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario ssh, written by:
#   certtool --scenario ssh --organization Acme --hostnames sftp.example.com,bastion.example.com --clients alice,backup --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/ssh.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario ssh: SSH keys for SSH, SFTP, SCP, and rsync: host keys that clients pin in known_hosts, and user keys for authorized_keys.

# Host key for sftp.example.com. sshd_config: HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh-host-sftp-example-com.key, owned by root with mode 0600.
# Clients pin it, so the first connection is not a guess: add a line to ~/.ssh/known_hosts with sftp.example.com followed by the
# type and data in ssh-host-sftp-example-com.key.pub. SFTP and SCP clients, such as WinSCP and FileZilla, show the same key's fingerprint:
# ssh-keygen -lf ssh-host-sftp-example-com.key.pub.
# SSH uses only the key: certtool writes a certificate too, which SSH ignores. certtool does not make OpenSSH certificates
# (ssh-keygen -s), so each key is trusted on its own.
- commonName: sftp.example.com
  keyType: ECDSA-256
  # 10 years. SSH ignores it.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  hostnames:
    - sftp.example.com
  sshPublicKey: true
  filename: ssh-host-sftp-example-com
# Host key for bastion.example.com. sshd_config: HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh-host-bastion-example-com.key, owned by root with mode 0600.
# Clients pin it, so the first connection is not a guess: add a line to ~/.ssh/known_hosts with bastion.example.com followed by the
# type and data in ssh-host-bastion-example-com.key.pub. SFTP and SCP clients, such as WinSCP and FileZilla, show the same key's fingerprint:
# ssh-keygen -lf ssh-host-bastion-example-com.key.pub.
- commonName: bastion.example.com
  keyType: ECDSA-256
  # 10 years. SSH ignores it.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  hostnames:
    - bastion.example.com
  sshPublicKey: true
  filename: ssh-host-bastion-example-com
# Key of alice. On each server, append ssh-user-alice.key.pub to ~alice/.ssh/authorized_keys. Log in with
# ssh -i ssh-user-alice.key, sftp -i, scp -i, or rsync -e "ssh -i ssh-user-alice.key". For an account that may only transfer
# files, add to sshd_config: Match User alice with ForceCommand internal-sftp and ChrootDirectory. In authorized_keys,
# restrict automation keys with from="<addresses>",restrict before the key.
- commonName: alice
  keyType: ECDSA-256
  # SSH ignores it. To rotate the key, delete ssh-user-alice.crt and ssh-user-alice.key, then run the spec again.
  validity: 8760h
  organization: Acme
  sshPublicKey: true
  filename: ssh-user-alice
# Key of backup. On each server, append ssh-user-backup.key.pub to ~backup/.ssh/authorized_keys. Log in with
# ssh -i ssh-user-backup.key, sftp -i, scp -i, or rsync -e "ssh -i ssh-user-backup.key". For an account that may only transfer
# files, add to sshd_config: Match User backup with ForceCommand internal-sftp and ChrootDirectory. In authorized_keys,
# restrict automation keys with from="<addresses>",restrict before the key.
- commonName: backup
  keyType: ECDSA-256
  # SSH ignores it. To rotate the key, delete ssh-user-backup.crt and ssh-user-backup.key, then run the spec again.
  validity: 8760h
  organization: Acme
  sshPublicKey: true
  filename: ssh-user-backup
```

## ftps

A CA that signs an FTPS (FTP over TLS) server certificate and optional client certificates, for vsftpd, ProFTPD, and FileZilla Server.

- `--hostnames`: the names clients connect to the FTP server by.
- `--clients`: optional, the users that log in with a certificate.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario ftps --organization Acme --hostnames ftp.example.com --clients partner-upload --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/ftps.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario ftps, written by:
#   certtool --scenario ftps --organization Acme --hostnames ftp.example.com --clients partner-upload --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/ftps.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario ftps: A CA that signs an FTPS (FTP over TLS) server certificate and optional client certificates, for vsftpd, ProFTPD, and FileZilla Server.

# CA. Clients trust ftps-ca.crt: curl --ssl-reqd --cacert ftps-ca.crt, lftp set ssl:ca-file, or WinSCP's TLS options.
# For SFTP, which runs over SSH and uses no certificates, see --scenario ssh.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep ftps-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme FTPS CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: ftps-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - ftp.example.com
  children:
    # FTPS server certificate. vsftpd: ssl_enable=YES, rsa_cert_file and rsa_private_key_file, force_local_logins_ssl=YES and
    # force_local_data_ssl=YES. ProFTPD mod_tls: TLSEngine on, TLSRSACertificateFile and TLSRSACertificateKeyFile, TLSRequired on.
    # FileZilla Server: the certificate and key files under Server > Configure > FTP over TLS.
    # RSA, because some FTP servers only load RSA keys (vsftpd rsa_cert_file).
    - commonName: ftp.example.com
      keyType: RSA-2048
      # To renew, delete ftps-server.crt and ftps-server.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - ftp.example.com
      filename: ftps-server
    # Client certificate for partner-upload. vsftpd: require_cert=YES, validate_cert=YES, and ca_certs_file ftps-ca.crt.
    # ProFTPD: TLSVerifyClient on and TLSCACertificateFile ftps-ca.crt. curl: --cert ftps-client-partner-upload.crt --key ftps-client-partner-upload.key;
    # WinSCP: Advanced > TLS/SSL > Client certificate file takes ftps-client-partner-upload.pfx.
    - commonName: partner-upload
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: RSA-2048
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: ftps-client-partner-upload
```

## ios

A development CA for iPhone and iPad apps, a backend certificate that meets Apple's TLS rules, and client identities.

- `--hostnames`: the names of the backend the app connects to.
- `--clients`: optional, client identities for apps that use mutual TLS.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario ios --organization Acme --hostnames api.dev.example.com --clients test-device --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/ios.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario ios, written by:
#   certtool --scenario ios --organization Acme --hostnames api.dev.example.com --clients test-device --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/ios.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario ios: A development CA for iPhone and iPad apps, a backend certificate that meets Apple's TLS rules, and client identities.

# CA. On a device, AirDrop or email ios-ca.crt, install the profile in Settings, then turn on full trust in
# Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings. In the Simulator: xcrun simctl keychain booted add-root-cert ios-ca.crt.
# App Transport Security then accepts the backend without exceptions. Apps themselves are signed with certificates from Apple.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep ios-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme iOS Development CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: ios-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  # IP addresses are not limited, so certtool still adds 127.0.0.1; add permittedIPRanges to limit them.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - api.dev.example.com
  children:
    # Backend certificate. Apple platforms reject TLS server certificates that are valid for more than 825 days, lack the
    # name in hostnames, or have RSA keys under 2048 bits; this one is valid for 397 days.
    - commonName: api.dev.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete ios-server.crt and ios-server.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 9528h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - api.dev.example.com
      filename: ios-server
    # Client identity for test-device. The app loads ios-client-test-device.pfx with SecPKCS12Import, or a configuration profile installs it.
    # The .pfx uses the legacy format, which older iOS and macOS releases need to import it; give it a long random password.
    - commonName: test-device
      pfx: legacy
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: ios-client-test-device
```

## android

A development CA that Android apps trust through a network security config, a backend certificate, and client certificates.

- `--hostnames`: the names of the backend the app connects to; add 10.0.2.2 to reach the host from the emulator.
- `--clients`: optional, client certificates for apps that use mutual TLS.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario android --organization Acme --hostnames api.dev.example.com,10.0.2.2 --clients test-device --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/android.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario android, written by:
#   certtool --scenario android --organization Acme --hostnames api.dev.example.com,10.0.2.2 --clients test-device --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/android.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario android: A development CA that Android apps trust through a network security config, a backend certificate, and client certificates.

# CA. Android apps do not trust user-installed CAs. Copy android-ca.crt to res/raw/android_ca.crt (resource names
# cannot contain hyphens) and trust it in res/xml/network_security_config.xml, inside <debug-overrides> to keep it
# out of release builds: <trust-anchors><certificates src="@raw/android_ca"/></trust-anchors>.
# Its key signs every certificate below it: keep android-ca.key off the servers, and use it only to issue certificates.
- commonName: Acme Android Development CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  keyType: ECDSA-384
  # 10 years.
  validity: 87600h
  organization: Acme
  filename: android-ca
  # Name constraints: certificates below this CA may only use these names and their subdomains.
  # Add a domain before you issue a certificate for it; changing them later means regenerating the CA and everything below it.
  permittedDNSDomains:
    - api.dev.example.com
  # The IP addresses certificates below this CA may use.
  permittedIPRanges:
    - 10.0.2.2/32
  children:
    # Backend certificate. The emulator reaches the host machine at 10.0.2.2: pass it in --hostnames to use this from the emulator.
    - commonName: api.dev.example.com
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      # To renew, delete android-server.crt and android-server.key, then run the spec again.
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      hostnames:
        - api.dev.example.com
        - 10.0.2.2
      filename: android-server
    # Client certificate for test-device. Load android-client-test-device.pfx into a KeyStore of type PKCS12 for the app's SSLContext or
    # OkHttp client, or install it in Settings > Security > Encryption & credentials for the browser.
    - commonName: test-device
      pfx: modern
      pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
      keyType: ECDSA-256
      validity: 8760h
      organization: Acme
      filename: android-client-test-device
```

## android-signing

An Android app signing (upload) key in a PKCS#12 keystore, valid for 25 years.

- Always self-signed, so it cannot be combined with `--yubikey`.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario android-signing --organization Acme --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/android-signing.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario android-signing, written by:
#   certtool --scenario android-signing --organization Acme --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/android-signing.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario android-signing: An Android app signing (upload) key in a PKCS#12 keystore, valid for 25 years.

# Android app signing key, in the PKCS#12 keystore android-signing.pfx. Sign with
#   apksigner sign --ks android-signing.pfx --ks-type PKCS12 app.apk
# or in Gradle with storeFile file("android-signing.pfx") and storeType "pkcs12" in signingConfigs;
# keytool -list -keystore android-signing.pfx shows the key alias. With Play App Signing, register
# android-signing.crt as the upload certificate; without it, losing this key means the app can never be updated.
- commonName: Acme Android Upload Key
  codeSigning: true
  # The android target makes an RSA-4096 key unless keyType is set.
  target: android
  pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
  # 25 years: Android only accepts an update signed with the same key, so it must outlive the app.
  validity: 219000h
  organization: Acme
  filename: android-signing
```

## code-sign

A code signing certificate for Windows (signtool) or Linux (osslsigncode).

- `--target`: `windows10` (the default), `windows11`, `windows7`, or `linux`.

```bash
# CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD must hold the password for the .pfx files
certtool --scenario code-sign --organization Acme --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/code-sign.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario code-sign, written by:
#   certtool --scenario code-sign --organization Acme --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/code-sign.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario code-sign: A code signing certificate for Windows (signtool) or Linux (osslsigncode).

# Self-signed code signing certificate. Machines must trust code-sign.crt to accept what it signs.
# Anyone who has its key can sign code as you; see docs/use-cases/code-signing.md for signing and verifying.
# The key is also written to code-sign.pfx for signtool.
- commonName: Acme Code Signing
  codeSigning: true
  # windows7, windows10, windows11, or linux. The key type comes from the target unless keyType is set.
  target: windows10
  pfxPasswordEnv: CERTTOOL_PFX_PASSWORD
  validity: 26280h
  organization: Acme
  filename: code-sign
```

## proxy

A CA for a TLS-inspecting proxy (Squid, mitmproxy), which signs a certificate for each site on the fly.

```bash
certtool --scenario proxy --organization Acme --output-dir certs
```

It writes certs/proxy.yaml and generates the certificates in it:

```yaml
# certtool spec for --scenario proxy, written by:
#   certtool --scenario proxy --organization Acme --output-dir certs
# which also generated the certificates. To change them, edit this file, then run:
#   certtool --spec certs/proxy.yaml --output-dir certs
# Running it again reuses the certificates already in the output directory,
# so you can add entries later. Format: https://github.com/cloudfra/certtool/blob/main/docs/spec.md

# Scenario proxy: A CA for a TLS-inspecting proxy (Squid, mitmproxy), which signs a certificate for each site on the fly.

# CA for a TLS-inspecting proxy, which signs a certificate for every site its clients visit. Its key sits on the proxy
# and can impersonate any site to the machines that trust it: install proxy-ca.crt only on managed machines.
# Squid: tls-cert=proxy-ca.crt tls-key=proxy-ca.key on an ssl-bump http_port.
# mitmproxy: cat proxy-ca.key proxy-ca.crt > ~/.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca.pem
- commonName: Acme TLS Inspection CA
  certificateAuthority: true
  # RSA, which every proxy and client supports.
  keyType: RSA-2048
  validity: 26280h
  organization: Acme
  filename: proxy-ca
  # 0: the proxy may sign site certificates but not other CAs.
  maxPathLen: 0
```
